items.title: Linux on Nvidia RTX Spark laptops runs GPU at 35% speed due to encrypted power management firmware limiting clock to 780 MHz [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
items.summary:
Linux can be installed and run with GPU acceleration on Nvidia RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, but the GPU clock speed is locked to about 780 MHz when plugged in, compared to over 2 GHz on Windows. This slowdown is caused by an encrypted power management firmware component, Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework, which only the Windows driver can decrypt, resulting in significantly reduced inference performance on Linux.

Installing Linux requires workarounds for hardware support and memory allocation, as the laptop reserves most unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows allows adjusting this split. Benchmarks show Windows and Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) achieve around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model, while native Linux on the same hardware manages only about 14 tokens per second due to the clock speed limitation.

The practical solution currently is to use WSL, which maintains full GPU performance by leveraging the Windows driver stack. A permanent fix depends on Nvidia porting the platform controller's power management logic to Linux drivers, which would enable full GPU speed and unlock the laptop's potential as a portable AI development platform.

items.title: Anthropic launches FlashProve prototype using cryptography to verify AI model responses without revealing model weights [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic's new prototype proves which model wrote an AI response without exposing its weights
items.summary:
Anthropic has introduced FlashProve, an open-source research prototype that uses zkSNARK cryptographic proofs to verify whether a specific AI model generated a given response without exposing the model's weights. The system aims to prevent model substitution or tampering by providing a digital fingerprint and proof for each output, although it currently supports only limited context lengths and deterministic outputs.

FlashProve generates proofs at about 110 tokens per second on a single GPU for Meta's Llama 4 Maverick model, producing proofs around 19 megabytes in size that can be verified in 17 seconds on a CPU. While this adds significant overhead compared to normal inference, it is a major improvement over previous methods that took hours and produced much larger proofs. Anthropic envisions uses such as regulatory verification of deployed models, safety audits, and tampering detection.

The prototype has limitations including a maximum context window of 1,024 tokens, inability to hide model architecture, and support only for the most likely token outputs rather than randomized sampling typical in chatbots. The code and documentation are available under an open-source license on GitHub.

items.summary:
Democrats secured control of both chambers of the US Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, driven by voter dissatisfaction with the economy and the war in Iran. The elections also highlighted growing political contention over AI data centers, with both parties opposing their expansion in some regions. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa was elected governor and pledged a moratorium on data center construction, reflecting broader concerns about AI infrastructure's local impact.

The opposition to data centers contrasts with earlier enthusiasm during the internet boom, as communities now have more say in permitting amid fears about AI's economic and societal effects. This shift marks a new dynamic where voters influence AI-related infrastructure decisions, unlike previous economic disruptions such as globalization, which often left affected workers without a voice. The debate over data centers underscores the complex intersection of technology, politics, and local economies in the AI era.

items.originalSummary:
Last week, SpaceX’s announcement that it would lease $40 billion worth of Nvidia Vera Rubin chips was a further signal of Elon Musk’s grand ambitions in the AI race. The deal also underscores the arrival of a new big player in that competition: Apollo Global Management, a 36-year-old private-equity pioneer turned private-lending giant.

items.originalTitle: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
items.summary:
The UK government has acknowledged that its previously cited estimate of AI adding £400 billion to the economy by 2030 was based on a report commissioned by Google and is significantly higher than its own projections. AI minister Kanishka Narayan stated the government’s more recent and uncertain estimate ranges from £55 billion to £140 billion, centering around £120 billion, reflecting slower AI adoption and data investment than initially assumed.

The disparity between the figures has been attributed to differing assumptions about the pace of AI adoption, with consultancy PF Global noting that government models assume a slower uptake than their 2023 projections. Despite ministers having access to the lower estimate since late 2025, the higher figure continued to be used publicly for months. Critics have called for greater transparency and independent research to ensure realistic expectations and effective policy-making around AI’s economic impact.

items.title: Should OpenAI Be Afraid of Jensen Huang? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Should OpenAI Be Afraid of Jensen Huang?
items.summary:
News flash: A lot of people in Silicon Valley are afraid of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

They have understandable reasons to be fearful, as Leo, Phoebe and I detailed in our story this morning. The chipmaker has a lot of money and influence to throw around, since Huang has the ear of several top government officials, including President Trump. 

More importantly for model developers like OpenAI, Nvidia controls the flow of AI chips they need to develop and run today’s most advanced models. It’s been hard enough for AI developers to get access to those chips, so it makes sense that the companies would want to avoid anything that might upset Huang.

This has led to a situation where OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the current debate over chip sales to China for fear of alienating Nvidia and Huang, which generates plenty of revenue from Chinese companies and wants access to the Chinese market itself. (Nvidia isn’t allowed to sell its most advanced tech directly to that market, but Chinese firms like ByteDance and DeepSeek still find a way to access the chips outside China’s borders or through smuggled hardware.)

items.originalTitle: How Nvidia Uses Its Soft Power to Influence Customers and Shape Policy
items.summary:
Last month, OpenAI Senior Research Scientist Noam Brown posted a link in a company Slack channel to a news story about OpenAI’s changing stance on advanced chip sales to China and asked a blunt question: “What is our policy on chip exports?” OpenAI policy leaders responded on Slack by citing past company posts, such as a safety blueprint on frontier AI published in June, that supported general chip export controls but did not address China specifically. They also directed staffers to speak to members of the global affairs team working on new export control policies, rather than discussing it on Slack.

Chip restrictions are a delicate topic at the company. Over the past year, OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the issue of chip export controls for China because OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, have expressed concern that doing so will alienate chipmaker Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, according to people with knowledge of the company’s strategy. Last year, as Congress turned its attention to export control legislation, a senior OpenAI policy staffer privately said OpenAI was not as vocal on chip export controls as it had been under the Biden administration because it feared antagonizing Huang and Nvidia, according to a staffer on Capitol Hill.

evidence: Title: 'The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests'
Summary: 'How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check'
Article: 'A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.'
Article: 'President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”'

importance.development_summary: Researchers propose "reverse game theory" as a conceptual approach to incentivize AI agents to follow rules. The approach is theoretical and not yet proven in practical enterprise deployments. Additionally, a political rebranding of AI as "Super Intelligence" is emerging as a loyalty signal within government contexts, but with limited enterprise impact currently.
importance.recommended_action: Monitor for follow-up evidence, adoption, vendor support, or regulatory movement.
importance.rationale: The story discusses conceptual research on controlling AI agents and a political rebranding of AI terminology, neither of which currently force changes in enterprise architecture, governance, or operations. There is low immediate risk and no production-ready technology or standards presented. Confidence is moderate due to credible reporting but lack of deployment evidence, so monitoring is appropriate.
watch_items: Demonstration of reverse game theory in production AI systems with enterprise controls
Wider adoption or enforcement of the "Super Intelligence" terminology affecting government or regulated entities
Emergence of governance or security frameworks based on these concepts
importance.business_rationale: The developments are primarily conceptual and political, with no clear immediate impact on enterprise business strategy, budgets, or operations.
importance.technical_rationale: The reverse game theory approach is still research-level without production deployment or integration implications, and the political terminology change does not affect technical architecture or platform strategy.
